new_statements.quote: [p.1] Pimbwe has seven vowel phonemes {i, ɪ, ɛ, a, ɔ, ʊ, u} and 23 consonant phonemes (see §2.1). It is a tonal language with three lexical tone categories for nouns and two lexical tone categories for verbs. Grammatical tone is also present. [...] [p.10, §2.2] Hyman (2003:48) mentions “five sources of vowel length in Bantu” languages: (1) underlying representation (phonemic vowel length), (2) vowel concatenation, (3) gliding plus compensatory lengthening, (4) compensatory lengthening preceding a moraic nasal plus consonant, and (5) penultimate vowel lengthening. Pimbwe exhibits all five of the aforementioned sources of vowel length.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The only modern description treats Pimbwe as a tone language (lexical + grammatical tone, phonemic vowel length) and gives no word-stress or accent statement; the sole prominence-related remark is that Pimbwe shows penultimate vowel lengthening (one of Hyman's five Bantu length sources), stated without examples, domain, or any link to stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None; penultimate lengthening is asserted in one sentence and not analysed further (the book groups sources 2-5 as 'compensatory lengthening').
new_statements.domain_note: Tone patterns are described for words in isolation (citation forms, Praat traces from one female speaker). The domain of the penultimate lengthening (word vs phrase/utterance) is not stated.
new_statements.identity_note: Weiss 2023 describes Pimbwe (ISO piw, Guthrie M.11, glottocode pimb1238) as spoken in the Katavi Region, western Tanzania; texts and pitch data from speakers at Usevya (Mpimbwe area). No dialect split is described; Rungwa (rnw) is named as the closest relative but is not covered. Same languoid as the target.

sources.note: Ch.2 Phonology (phonemes, vowel length, syllable types, tone, processes). The words 'stress' and 'accent' never occur. States Pimbwe is a tonal language (3 lexical tone categories for nouns, 2 for verbs, plus grammatical tone; p.1 and section 2.5 pp.13-21, surface tones only). Section 2.2 (p.10) says Pimbwe exhibits all five of Hyman's (2003) Bantu sources of vowel length, including '(5) penultimate vowel lengthening', which it lumps under 'compensatory lengthening' without further discussion. No statement of where word stress/prominence falls.
